newsitem.title: USA: Hispanics stage first major march in Washington.
newsitem.headline: Hispanics stage first major march in Washington.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Hispanics on Saturday staged their first major march in Washington to protest against immigration and welfare reforms they view as a racist backlash against their community.
Waving U.S. and Latin American flags and chanting slogans in Spanish, the demonstrators marched from a predominantly Hispanic neighbourhood to the Ellipse park behind the White House for a rally.
While organisers' tallies of the crowd varied from 50,000 to 80,000 people, Park Police officers refused to offer their estimate.
"We're here for the millions who wanted to come and could not be here," said one of the main organisers, immigrants' rights advocate Juan Jose Gutierrez. "A united people will never be defeated."

The demonstration, largely the idea of young and radical grassroots activists like Gutierrez, attracted participants ranging from minimum wage earners to students wearing "Che" Guevara t-shirts and federal legislators, as well as a few celebrities such as talk show host Geraldo Rivera.
"This is a historic day for Latinos. This is our Million Man March," enthused Rivera, referring to a much larger demonstration staged last year by blacks in Washington.

One after another, speakers at the rally rejected welfare and immigration reforms approved this year by the Republican-controlled Congress, as well as proposals to make English as the official language of the United States.

"To the politicians who supported those proposals we say: please, don't be hypocrites. Don't run advertisements in Spanish now to try to get our votes," said Representative Jose Serrano, a New York Democrat of Puerto Rican extraction.
Latino advocates hold that, even though Hispanics are bound to overtake blacks early next century as the largest racial minority in the United States, they are still politically under-represented.
They also feel that their community has been turned into a scapegoat in this electoral year, simply because they are the latest and poorest immigrants to arrive in the United States.

"What unites us now is not only the struggle for civil rights. It's a hunger for respect," said Raul Yzaguirre, president of the National Council of La Raza, one of the leading Latino advocacy groups.
In response to the new laws limiting foreign-born residents' access to social services, hundreds of thousands of Hispanics have become U.S. citizens over the past year.
Such was the case of Elsa Torres, a Washington house cleaner of who came from Guatemala 18 years ago as an illegal immigrant, and her Salvadoran-born husband, Nelson Torres.
"We did it to make sure we have rights, to be able to vote and to make our voices heard," she said as she marched.
Representative Ed Pastor, an Arizona Democrat and chairman of the Hispanic Caucus in Congress, said the next challenge would be to get out the Latino vote on the Nov. 5 election.
"The Hispanic community must go to the polls to say that it won't tolerate to see its rights trampled on," he said.

Hispanics, who in the past were less likely to vote than white and black Americans, traditionally support Democratic candidates in states like California, Texas, New York and Illinois, and favour Republicans in Florida.
